analysis.one_liner: Temporarily suspends USDA waivers letting meat and poultry plants run faster processing lines during COVID-19.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have rolled back faster slaughterhouse line speeds during the pandemic, was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in July 2020 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the pandemic, the Department of Agriculture had granted meat and poultry plants waivers to speed up their processing lines and had approved a new swine inspection system. This bill would have suspended those waivers and blocked any new line-speed increases until 90 days after the COVID-19 emergency ended, and directed federal agencies to report to Congress and the Government Accountability Office on how well they protected meat plant workers, animals, and food safety during the pandemic.
analysis.who_benefits: Meatpacking workers, who faced some of the worst COVID-19 outbreaks of any industry while working shoulder to shoulder on fast-moving processing lines, and federal food-safety inspectors stationed at those plants. Faster lines give workers less time to do each task and less ability to keep distance from coworkers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill suspends all existing waivers and bars new ones related to line speeds and inspection staffing at meat and poultry plants for the covered period, ending through 90 days after the COVID-19 emergency is lifted [S2][S3].
It also suspends implementation of and conversion to the New Swine Slaughter Inspection System, the 2019 rule that allowed faster slaughter line speeds at pork plants [S2][S3].
It prohibits USDA from spending any funds on any policy or program that would increase line speeds at covered plants during the covered period [S2][S3].

It requires the Agriculture, Labor, and Health and Human Services departments to report to Congress by the end of 2020 on actions taken to protect workers, animals, and food during the pandemic, and directs the Government Accountability Office to review those actions, including the impact of faster line speeds on worker protections and any interference with CDC investigations of plant outbreaks [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large meat and poultry processing companies, which would lose the faster line speeds the Agriculture Department had allowed them, reducing how many animals they can process per day until the suspension expires.

drawbacks.text: Slower line speeds mean less throughput for meat processors, which industry argued raised costs and could affect meat supply and prices for consumers [S3].
The bill is temporary by design: the suspensions end 90 days after the COVID-19 emergency is lifted, so it does not permanently resolve the line-speed policy question [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is worker safety against plant throughput. Faster lines were granted as waivers and a rule change, and the bill simply returns to the pre-waiver status quo until shortly after the emergency ends, while ordering an audit of how agencies handled worker protection during the pandemic. The cost falls on processors' efficiency; the benefit goes to workers in plants that saw severe COVID-19 outbreaks. As a temporary emergency measure with a built-in review, the design is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which took no action on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on July 28, 2020, with six original Senate cosponsors including Mr. Blumenthal, Mr. Merkley, Mrs. Feinstein, Ms. Warren, Mr. Sanders, and Ms. Harris [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S1][S5].
No further action was taken: the committee never held a markup or brought the bill to the floor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meat and poultry processors kept the faster line-speed waivers and the new swine inspection system that the bill would have suspended, and meatpacking workers got no relief from faster lines during the pandemic.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to suspend line-speed waivers during the pandemic.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 28, 2020 and took no action; no markup, hearing, or floor consideration followed before the Congress ended.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.what_they_did: Favored keeping the faster line speeds and the new swine inspection system the bill would have suspended.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows how other senators would have lined up.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped their USDA-granted line-speed waivers and paused the new swine inspection system, slowing slaughter and processing lines. Faster lines raise throughput but reduce workers' time per task and their ability to keep distance, which mattered greatly during COVID-19 outbreaks in plants.
Suspending staffing-relief waivers would have restored fuller inspection staffing at covered plants, and the bill ordered an audit of protections for inspectors during the pandemic.
